summary: Isoamyl 2-cyanoacrylate is a synthetic liquid tissue adhesive (surgical glue) supplied as a medical device. On contact with moisture or tissue surfaces it undergoes rapid exothermic polymerisation to form a strong, flexible adhesive film, providing wound closure and haemostasis. The longer isoamyl (5-carbon) ester offers better tensile strength, flexibility and lower tissue toxicity than shorter-chain cyanoacrylates. It is used topically for skin and intraoral wound closure and, by injection, for endoscopic obturation of gastric/oesophageal varices and embolisation of vascular lesions.
indications: Topical closure of minor lacerations and surgical incisions (skin, in place of or with sutures)
Intraoral/mucosal wound closure (e.g. after extraction of impacted teeth, periapical surgery, cleft repair)
Haemostasis and sealing of bleeding tissue surfaces
Embolisation of varicocele and selected vascular lesions

dosage.d: Thin layer applied across approximated edges
dosage.t: Apply 1-3 thin coats, allowing each to polymerise
dosage.n: Hold edges apposed; keep glue out of the wound itself and off surrounding healthy areas

dosage.t: Apply to dry field; allow to set
dosage.n: Achieve haemostasis and dry the field first

dosage.d: Small aliquots (e.g. ~0.5-1 mL per injection) by trained endoscopist
dosage.t: Injected then flushed (e.g. with distilled water/saline)
dosage.n: Specialist procedure; avoid premature catheter polymerisation

dosage.d: Volume per lesion at operator discretion

admin: External / device use - never for systemic administration
Ensure the tissue field is dry and bleeding controlled before application
Apply a thin layer to approximated edges; do not place adhesive within the wound or between non-apposed surfaces
Allow polymerisation (seconds) before releasing tension; build up in thin layers rather than one thick blob
Avoid contact with gloves, instruments, eyes and unintended tissue (it bonds rapidly); protect surrounding skin
Injection/embolisation techniques are specialist procedures performed under appropriate imaging/endoscopic guidance
moa: The cyanoacrylate monomer undergoes rapid anionic polymerisation when it contacts the hydroxyl ions of water/tissue moisture, forming a solid polymer film that mechanically bonds tissue surfaces and seals them. The reaction is exothermic. The isoamyl (longer-chain) ester degrades more slowly and produces less formaldehyde/cyanoacetate on breakdown than short-chain cyanoacrylates, giving lower histotoxicity, greater flexibility and good tensile strength. It also provides a physical barrier with bacteriostatic and haemostatic effects.

absolute: Application to infected, contaminated or actively suppurating wounds
Use within the wound cavity or on mucosal surfaces not intended for the product
Contact with eyes (unless an ophthalmic-specific product/indication)
relative: Wounds under high tension or across joints/mobile areas (may need sutures)
Areas of high moisture or constant friction
Deep or gaping wounds requiring layered closure
Vascular procedures without appropriate operator expertise/imaging
monitor: Signs of local infection or inflammation
For embolic use: non-target embolisation under imaging

preg: Not systemically absorbed when used topically, so systemic fetal exposure is not expected; use for surgical wound closure as clinically indicated.
lact: Not systemically absorbed with topical use; compatible with breastfeeding.
renal: Not applicable - topical/local device that is not systemically absorbed; no renal handling.
hepatic: Not applicable - topical/local device that is not systemically absorbed; no hepatic metabolism of clinical relevance.

interactions.alcohol: Not applicable; note adhesive and solvents may be flammable - keep from ignition sources/cautery until set
interactions.diagnostics: Polymerised cyanoacrylate used for embolisation/varix obturation may be visible or cause artefact on subsequent imaging

common: Transient stinging or warmth on application (exothermic polymerisation)
Mild local inflammation at the application site
serious: Wound dehiscence if used on high-tension or inappropriate wounds
Local infection if applied to contaminated tissue
For injection/embolisation: non-target embolisation, glue migration, embolic complications
rare: Inadvertent bonding of unintended surfaces (skin, eyelids)
emergency: Embolic complications (e.g. pulmonary embolisation) during vascular/variceal use

monitoring: Wound closure quality and apposition over healing
Local signs of infection, inflammation or rejection of the film
For variceal obturation/embolisation: procedural imaging and post-procedure surveillance for non-target embolisation
Spontaneous sloughing of the film as the wound heals (typically within days to ~1-2 weeks)
counsel: Keep the glued area clean and dry as advised; the film will slough off on its own as the wound heals
Do not pick, scrub or apply ointments/creams over the adhesive unless told to
Avoid prolonged soaking (long baths/swimming) until healed
Report increasing redness, swelling, pus, pain or if the wound opens
Brief stinging or warmth when applied is expected
pk: Polymerises and bonds within seconds of contact with tissue moisture
Not applicable - acts locally; not systemically absorbed
Not applicable - no systemic absorption; film degrades/sloughs locally over time
Adhesive film persists until wound healing, typically sloughing within days to ~1-2 weeks
Store cool and dry (often refrigerated per IFU), tightly sealed away from moisture; flammable - keep from heat/ignition; observe expiry
pearls: This is a tissue-adhesive MEDICAL DEVICE, not an FDA-approved systemic drug - information drawn from manufacturer Instructions for Use (e.g. Amcrylate) and clinical literature; regulatory clearance is as a device
Pharmacokinetics are essentially not applicable: it polymerises on contact with moisture/tissue and is not systemically absorbed
The longer isoamyl ester gives better flexibility, tensile strength and lower tissue toxicity than short-chain cyanoacrylates
Apply only to dry, approximated, non-infected edges - never inside the wound; build thin layers
Bonds rapidly to any moist surface - protect eyes, gloves and unintended skin; keep from cautery/ignition until set
missed: Not applicable - applied as needed during a procedure (single/topical use), so there is no missed-dose schedule.
overdose: Not applicable in the conventional sense; risk relates to misuse - excessive or misplaced application can cause thick brittle films, poor apposition, foreign-body reaction or, with intravascular use, non-target embolisation. Accidental skin/eyelid bonding should not be forced apart; soak and seek medical/ophthalmic help. Do not ingest or inject outside the intended technique.
